title: the daily routine (dinacharya)
hook: the streetlights come on and, in some homes, a small lamp too: the day has joints, and the routine marks them

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daily routine reached past the skin: sadvritta, good conduct, and greeting first, with a friendly face.

Dusk, and the streetlights blink on one after another down the block. In some Hindu homes, around the same moment, someone lights a small lamp in front of the family shrine. Nobody announces it. The light outside is changing, so the light inside is changed too. Back on day one hundred eighteen, the path met these joints of the day, the hours of sandhya. On the last day of the daily round, it meets them again, along with what to do when life bends the routine.
screen: `STREETLIGHTS, AND A SMALL LAMP.` → `THE DAY HAS JOINTS.` → `WHEN LIFE BENDS THE ROUTINE.`

segments.voice: Sandhya is a joining, a twilight, the meeting point of two parts of the day. Some Hindus keep prayers at these meeting points, called sandhyavandana, honoring the junctions, at dawn and at dusk, and for some at noon too. Lamps lit at dusk come from the same attention. The Ayurvedic texts notice the joints from another side. Among its rules of good conduct, paraphrased, the Charaka Samhita advises against eating, sleeping or studying at the twilights. Whatever the reasons a reader finds there, the effect is the same: the joints of the day are kept a little apart, a little quieter. So the round, which began before sunrise, has shape all day: a waking, the senses, the oil, effort in measure, kind speech, and pauses at the turns. Now the honest part. Plenty of lives don't fit a dawn-to-dusk shape. Night shifts. A newborn. Illness. A job that starts at four. Does the routine just break? Read closely, the texts already leave room. The verse about waking addressed the healthy person. Exercise was measured to strength and season. And in the Ashtanga Hridaya, the chapter after the day is the year: how the routine changes with the seasons. A routine that changes with the year isn't a rigid one. So when life bends the schedule, keep the pieces that fit, and mark the joints you actually have: waking, a meal, the end of a shift. The routine follows the person, the way the texts follow the season.
screen: `SANDHYA: THE DAY'S JOINTS` · `KEEP THE JOINTS A LITTLE QUIET` · `PLENTY OF LIVES DON'T FIT` · `THE ROUTINE FOLLOWS THE PERSON`

segments.voice: Walk through a usual day, yours, not an ideal one, and find where one part bends into the next: waking, leaving the house, a meal, coming home, the last light switched off. Choose one of those joints and see yourself pausing there for a single breath before going on. If you pray, a prayer you already know can mark that joint.
The daily routine. Dinacharya, the day's conduct, from waking to the twilight, built to bend to the person who keeps it.
Your line: the daily routine, dinacharya. A pause at the joints your day really has. That's today, done.
